title: Why Japan Gets So Many Earthquakes: M5.7 Quake Shakes Shizuoka
fb_caption: Just after 1 a.m. on 8 November 2026, a magnitude 5.7 earthquake (Japan Meteorological Agency) struck western Shizuoka Prefecture in central Japan, about 40 km deep. No tsunami warning was issued. So why does Japan shake so often? Four tectonic plates, subduction zones and around 2,000 known active faults, plus how Japan prepares and what to do if you ever feel a quake. Did you know Japan shakes this often? Tell us below.
engagement_comment: Quick poll: have you ever felt an earthquake? Reply 1 = yes, more than once, 2 = once, 3 = never (and hoping to keep it that way!)

Explainer (general, not about this quake): Japan sits where four plates meet (Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian/Amurian, North American/Okhotsk), standard plate-tectonics teaching (USGS, JMA).

'More than 1 in 10 of the world's M6+ earthquakes': Cabinet Office of Japan, White Paper on Disaster Management: 302 of 1,629 M6.0+ quakes = 18.5% (2004-2013, via nippon.com 'Nearly 20% of large earthquakes happen in Japan'); Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications white paper: about 13.1% (2008-2018). The video says 'more than 1 in 10', which both support. 'Under 1% of the world's land': nippon.com gives 0.28%.
'Around 2,000 known active faults': Headquarters for Earthquake Research Promotion (HERP) commonly cited figure; NOT re-fetched by the builder, verify before posting.
Earthquake Early Warning: JMA alerts can arrive seconds before strong shaking (general knowledge, NOT re-fetched).
Drop, Cover and Hold On: standard earthquake safety advice (e.g. US Ready.gov / ShakeOut).

beats.text: Just after 1 a.m. on November 8th, a magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck western Shizuoka Prefecture in central Japan. Shaking was felt in Aichi, Nagano and Gifu. So why does Japan shake so often?
Japan covers well under 1% of the world's land. Yet it gets more than 1 in 10 of the world's magnitude 6 or bigger earthquakes. Here are the three big reasons.
One. Location. Japan sits where four tectonic plates meet. The Pacific, the Philippine Sea, the Eurasian, and the North American plates.
Two. Subduction. Off Japan's coast, one plate dives underneath another. But it doesn't slide smoothly. The edges get stuck, and strain builds up, year after year.
Think of bending a plastic ruler. It bends, and bends, storing energy, until it suddenly snaps back. That snap is an earthquake, and the energy races out as seismic waves.

Three. All that pushing cracks the land above, into around 2,000 known active faults. Quakes also vary in depth. Deeper ones, like this one at about 40 kilometres, usually spread shaking wider, but weaker.
So how does Japan cope? Strict building codes. Many tall buildings sit on rubber base isolators or dampers, so they sway gently instead of shaking hard.
And phones get early warning alerts, sometimes seconds before strong shaking arrives. Enough time to take cover.
If you ever feel a quake, remember three words. Drop to the ground. Take cover under a sturdy table. And hold on until the shaking stops.
Did you know Japan shakes this often? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone heading to Japan. Because there, the ground never stops moving. Just like in Shizuoka, on November 8th.
